text:
Education in Greece is a concurrent responsibility of the state and local authorities, characterized by a compulsory nine-year system comprising six years of primary school and three years of lower secondary education (Gymnasium). Preschool education, lasting two years, is mandatory for children aged 4 to 6, while primary school follows a 6-year cycle with automatic progression to the Gymnasium. The Gymnasium, attended from ages 12 to 15, is the gateway to upper secondary education. Following this, students attend the Lyceum (upper secondary school) for three non-compulsory years (ages 15 to 18), culminating in the "Apolytirio Lykeiou" (high school diploma). Admission to higher education requires passing the national Pan-Hellenic Examinations, where students select specific subjects based on their Lyceum stream, with scores weighted to determine university placement.
The system is highly structured with various school types, including General Lyceums, Vocational Lyceums (EPAL), Model Lyceums, and Art/Music Lyceums, allowing for specialization in fields such as technology, humanities, and crafts. Vocational training is integrated through dual-education programs like the Post-High School Year Apprenticeship Class, which combines workplace training with school instruction to lead to Level 5 qualifications. Higher education is primarily provided by public Higher Education Institutes (HEIs), which offer free tuition for undergraduate studies, though postgraduate programs often require fees. The National Qualification Framework (HQF) aligns Greek qualifications with international standards, while non-formal education options include digital platforms, open courses, and lifelong learning centers. Despite high literacy rates, challenges persist regarding corruption, bullying, and the need for continuous reform to ensure educational quality and equity.
